Writing by Hand in Class

Most of the writing you do for this course happens in class, by hand, without your notes. This page is about how to do that well.

These are guidelines, not an assignment description. The exercises vary: sometimes short answers to several questions, sometimes a longer essay on a topic you choose. How much of what follows applies will depend on the exercise, and I will tell you what each one asks for.

For the formal take-home essay, see the Writing Guidelines. A good deal of what is there holds here too, in relaxed form — and where it relaxes, this page says so.

An Artificial Exercise, on Purpose

Nobody writes history this way. Real historical work is slow. The sources sit open on the desk, you go back and check, you discover on the third pass that the thing you were sure of on the first was wrong. Writing from memory against a clock is nothing like the actual practice of the discipline.

So why do it? Partly for the obvious reason: these conditions are hard to outsource (see AI in This Course). But mostly because the artifice isolates something worth isolating.

Think about what a citation actually involves. First, knowing which source bears on your argument and what it shows. Second, finding the page and formatting the note. The second half is now something software does in seconds — hand a machine a scan of your handwriting and a set of detailed notes and it will give you back a properly footnoted essay. The first half it cannot do for you, because it requires having read the thing and understood why it matters.

These exercises test the first half. Not whether you memorized, but whether you can take what you genuinely absorbed and put a claim on the page with evidence under it, cold. That is the part of the skill that stays yours, and it is what makes the slow, careful version possible later.

You will know some things, and reasonably should, having just done the reading and watched the lecture (see Course Format and Materials). But recall is the floor here, not the point. The point is what you do with it.

What Matters Most, in Order

When the clock runs out — and it will — spend your remaining minutes in this order:

  1. Argument and evidence. A claim, and something sourced holding it up.
  2. Structure. Enough that a reader can follow you.
  3. Style. Try, but do not bleed for it.

So if you have five minutes left, add evidence, not polish. An argument with a source behind it and a clumsy sentence beats an elegant paragraph resting on nothing.

I do not count words. People write at very different speeds, and length is not the measure. A short, tight response that makes one well-grounded point is worth more than three rambling pages.

Citing Without Your Notes

The principle is not a formality. Historians rest their claims on evidence and say where it came from, so that a reader can go and check. That is the discipline’s basic honesty, and it does not switch off because you are writing by hand.

What changes is the form, which relaxes a long way. Page numbers are essentially out of the question here — do not spend a second trying to recall one. What I am looking for is simply enough that I can tell which source you mean.

In descending order of usefulness, all of these work:

  • The author or title, if you have it: (Radishchev).
  • The session number, if that is what stuck: (13.2), meaning the second reading for session 13. Perfectly good — though do not go memorizing numbers, which matter only as labels.
  • A description: (that assigned reading by the Russian Enlightenment intellectual). I will almost certainly know what you mean.
  • For a recorded lecture: the number, or just (the lecture where you talked about the grain requisitions).
  • An honest blank: (a primary source from this unit, I can’t recall which).

More specific is better. Vague is far better than nothing. Inventing a source is worse than nothing — if you cannot place it, say so, exactly as in the last example above.

If a quotation has genuinely stuck with you, use it: put it in quotation marks and mark it as (approximate quotation). That tells me you are reproducing from memory rather than claiming exactness.

Here is the whole thing in practice. Suppose you want to argue that Russian Enlightenment intellectuals were in constant communication with their French counterparts. In a formal essay you would want a Chicago footnote, author, title, page. Here, this does the job:

Russian Enlightenment thinkers were in sustained contact with the French philosophes, and read themselves as participants in the same argument rather than observers of it (that assigned reading by the Russian Enlightenment intellectual).

The claim is grounded, the source is identifiable, and you have shown you engaged with the reading. That is all the citation needs to accomplish here.

No footnotes. Parenthetical references only.

Why Primary Sources Still Come First

The Writing Guidelines ask you to prioritize primary sources, then secondary scholarship, then textbooks, then lectures. That order is not a classroom convention; it is a methodological principle. The closer you get to the evidence itself, the more of the interpretive work you are doing yourself, and the more your argument is yours rather than borrowed.

In this format, the order inverts in practice, and I know it. The lecture you watched last night is what you remember most precisely; the primary source, read once and set down, is what you remember least. So the standard is relaxed: a half-remembered primary source cited loosely is worth more here than a crisply recalled line from the textbook.

But the target does not move. The commonest weakness in work like this is an answer written entirely out of lecture and textbook, with the primary sources untouched — and it is visible immediately, because the argument has nothing in it that could only have come from the evidence. Reach for the source even when your grip on it is imperfect.

Why a Range of Sources Is Better

Putting two sources beside each other, especially two that do not agree, is where historical argument actually lives. One source tells you what someone claimed; two tell you there was something to argue about. In a take-home essay, engaging a diverse body of evidence is an expectation.

Here it is often simply not practical, and I am not setting a quota. One source used well beats three name-dropped. But if a second thing you read pulls against the first, saying so is the most valuable sentence you can write.

Format: What Scales Down

  • Lead with your claim. The Writing Guidelines put this as “frontload key insights”; under a clock it becomes the whole of structural advice. First sentence, say what you are arguing.
  • You may label it. Writing “Thesis:” and then your claim is something you would never do in a formal essay, and is perfectly welcome here. Not required.
  • A thesis may be listy. The connective-tissue standard — a thesis that finds the larger theme uniting the body paragraphs — is a take-home aspiration. Here, a thesis that simply names what you are going to argue is fine.
  • Outline first, and leave it on the page. Two minutes of outlining before you write is the highest-return thing you can do, and the outline itself is not a mess to be hidden. Crossed-out or not, it shows your reasoning.
  • A missing conclusion is no great loss. If you run out of time, do not scramble for a tidy ending. Outline what you would have argued, or add a few bullets naming the primary sources you would have brought in. That tells me what you knew and where you were going.
  • One sentence of counter-argument is the best value available. Naming the strongest objection to your own claim costs almost nothing and does more for a response than a concluding paragraph.
  • First person is fine — “I argue that” — but this is still not a venue for personal opinion. You are persuading a reader about a shared body of evidence.
  • Define your terms, briefly, where a term is doing real work.
  • How much latitude you have over the topic varies by exercise. A take-home essay prompt is only a prompt and you set your own scope; a short answer to a specific question should answer that question. When an exercise lets you choose, I will say so.

Visible Process Is Fine

This is a handwritten draft, not a fair copy, and it may look like one.

Cross things out. Write notes to yourself in the margin. Draw an arrow showing that two paragraphs should swap places, instead of recopying them. Add a line at the bottom saying what you would have checked if you had the book. None of that counts against you; some of it counts for you, because it shows a mind at work rather than a performance of fluency.

Two practical matters live elsewhere: if I cannot read your handwriting, see the FAQ in Grading Policies — it is not a problem, and nobody is penalized for penmanship. For scanning and uploading your pages, see What to Bring in Course Format and Materials.

The Genre Trap

The most common way these responses go wrong is not a bad argument. It is writing in the wrong genre altogether, usually one of three:

  • The personal reflection — what the material made you feel or think about your own life.
  • The polemic — a strong opinion with no evidence under it.
  • The summary — a competent narration of what happened, with no argument at all.

The third is the one to watch, because under time pressure it is the path of least resistance. Narration is what you can produce without deciding anything. Writing “X happened, then Y happened” requires no judgment, which is exactly why it feels safe when the clock is running and exactly why it earns little.

These are all real and valuable kinds of writing. They are not what this exercise asks for, and the distinction is not an arbitrary classroom rule. Being able to tell an argument from a summary — in your own writing and in everyone else’s — is most of what historical training is for. It is what lets you read a work of scholarship and see what it is claiming rather than only what it is describing.

The fix is small: find the sentence in your response that someone could disagree with. If there isn’t one, you have written a summary.
